You're right, and that's a bad error to make three times. "After the last frost in May" is Northern Hemisphere advice read off a calendar, and in Dunedin it would have you sowing beans into late autumn. I'm sorry — and it's worse that you only caught it because of thirty years' experience, because your daughter won't have that.

I can't see what I've said to you before from here, so I can't audit the specific conversations. What I can do is tell you the categories of advice that most often come out inverted or wrong for Otago, so you (and she) know where to check:

**Things that flip with the hemisphere**
- Any month named for a task: "sow in March", "plant garlic in October", "prune roses in February". Shift six months, then sanity-check against local conditions rather than trusting the arithmetic.
- Frost dates. Dunedin's last frost is realistically October into early November on the hill suburbs, and first frosts can arrive in April. "Plant tomatoes out after Labour Weekend" is the local rule of thumb for a reason.
- Spring/autumn bulb and seed-potato timing, garlic (shortest day in, longest day out — in NZ that's June in, December out), and anything keyed to daylength.
- Orientation advice: "south-facing wall for warmth" is wrong here; it's north-facing you want.
- Pest and disease calendars: codling moth, white butterfly, aphid flushes all follow our seasons, not theirs.

**Things that don't flip but are still wrong for Dunedin specifically**
- Most online growing advice assumes a warmer, longer summer than Dunedin gets. Days-to-maturity on packets is honest, but "summer" here is short and cool and maritime — more like coastal Scotland than Auckland. Heat-lovers (capsicums, aubergines, melons, some tomatoes) often need a tunnel house or won't crop reliably outdoors.
- "Full sun" recommendations don't account for a low winter sun angle and hill shading.

**Things that are safe to trust from anywhere**
- Sowing depth, spacing, thinning, watering principles, soil preparation, companion planting, how to harden off seedlings — none of that depends on where you are.

For your daughter, the simplest protection is a local source of truth to check against: the NZ sowing guides on the back of Yates or Kings seed packets (they're written for NZ regions, and Dunedin is "cool" zone), the Dunedin Botanic Garden, and the Otago/Southland gardening groups. A good habit: if advice names a month or a season, ask "is this written for here?" before acting on it.

If you want, paste the advice you're concerned about — or just tell me what you're both planning to grow and when — and I'll go through it line by line with Dunedin as the fixed point this time.

You've done the right things. The problem isn't that you haven't done enough — it's that a verbal request gets "we'll keep an eye on him," and a written one starts a legal clock. That's the change to make this week.

**Put the evaluation request in writing.** Under federal law (IDEA) and Ohio's rules, once you request an evaluation for a suspected disability in writing, the district has 30 days to either get your consent to evaluate or give you written notice explaining why they're refusing. If they evaluate, they have 60 days from your consent to complete it and meet with you. "Let's keep watching" is no longer an option once the letter exists. Send it to the principal and the school's special education coordinator (not just the teacher), by email so it's dated, and keep a copy. Something like:

"I am requesting a full and individual evaluation of my son, [name], grade 3 at [school], for special education eligibility under IDEA. I am concerned about his reading, including [specific: he cannot read a full sentence independently; this has been raised at conferences since kindergarten]. Please send me the consent form and the written notice required by Ohio Operating Standards. I understand the district has 30 days to respond to this request. Thank you."

**Two Ohio-specific things to ask about in the same email:**
- Ohio's Third Grade Reading Guarantee requires schools to assess every K-3 student and put any student who's not on track on a Reading Improvement and Monitoring Plan (RIMP). Ask whether he has one, and for a copy. If he's in third grade and can't read a sentence, he should.
- Ohio's dyslexia law requires schools to screen K-3 students for dyslexia. Ask for his screening results and what tier of intervention he's receiving. If the teacher's answer has been "late bloomer" since kindergarten, there may be no screening data at all, and that's worth knowing.

**If the district says no or stalls:** you can ask for an Independent Educational Evaluation at district expense, or get a private evaluation (a licensed psychologist or a university reading clinic; some are sliding-scale). The Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD) has free parent advocates who know the process and can help you with the letter or the meeting.

One honest note: "late bloomer" is a real thing for some kids in kindergarten and first grade. It is not a plausible explanation for a third grader who can't read a sentence. You are not overreacting.

The reason you're stuck is that the board's criterion and your job are pulling in different directions, and you can feel it. "Most likely to raise their grades" rewards picking the kids who are nearly there and don't need you much. The kids who most need a homework club are precisely the ones whose grades are hardest to move. Twelve names chosen by the board's rule will make a good annual report and quietly turn away the eight children the club exists for.

I'd do three things before Friday.

**1. Push back on the metric, briefly and in writing.** Not a fight — a sentence or two to the chair: "If we select on 'most likely to raise grades' we'll be choosing children who need us least, and reviewers of the report will spot that. I'd propose we select on need and report on attendance, homework completion and grade change for the cohort we actually serve." Boards usually accept this when it's framed as protecting the report's credibility.

**2. Try to not choose at all.** Twenty kids and one fewer tutor might still fit if you change the shape: two shorter sessions instead of one long one; a 2-day and 3-day cohort; pairing older or stronger kids as peer helpers for part of the session; a parent volunteer or a sixth-former/university student for one afternoon a week; asking the school whether a teaching assistant could be released. Losing one tutor doesn't have to mean losing eight places.

**3. If you genuinely have to pick twelve, pick on need and be transparent.** Criteria that hold up: no one at home who can help with homework; already behind; a teacher referral; younger kids (earlier intervention pays off more); and anyone who was in the club last term (continuity matters). Write the criteria down so you can show them. Then don't just drop the other eight: a named waitlist with a start date if a place opens, a weekly drop-in hour if you can run one, and a short note to each family with one concrete alternative (library homework help, school's own club, an online resource). Being told "not this term, here's when, here's what else" is a very different experience from silence.

If you tell me roughly who the twenty are (ages, who referred them, which ones you're most worried about), I'll help you build the list and the note to the board.

Short version of why: under UK261 (the UK's version of EU261), when your flight is cancelled the airline must offer you rerouting at the earliest opportunity or a refund. If they don't provide it and you have to arrange it yourself, you can claim the reasonable cost of the replacement ticket back from them. A £340 same-day fare on another carrier is reasonable. Fifty minutes on hold is your evidence that you gave them the chance.

Before you tap pay, 30 seconds:
1. Check the original airline's app or the "manage booking" page — sometimes they've already rebooked you and the app shows it even though the phone line doesn't.
2. Screenshot the cancellation notice and your call timer.
3. Keep the receipt for the new ticket, and for food/drink while you wait (also claimable).

Separately from the ticket cost, you may be owed fixed compensation (£350 for London–Lisbon distance) if the cancellation was within 14 days and wasn't "extraordinary circumstances" like weather or ATC. That claim doesn't depend on whether you self-booked.

Claim afterwards through the airline's online form; if they refuse, the CAA's ADR scheme or AviationADR. Go get your seat.

The thing that poisons Christmas isn't the loss, it's the ambiguity afterwards: was it a loan or a gift, when was it due, who else knows, and whether anyone's allowed to mention it. So the document should answer all of that in advance, including what happens on failure.

**Decide privately first:** how much of the ₦4.5m you could lose and still be fine. Honestly, mentally book that part as a gift now. Whatever's left is the part you'll actually hold him to.

**Simple loan agreement — between brothers, plain language:**

1. **Parties and amount.** [You] lends [Brother] ₦4,500,000 on [date], transferred to [account]. Purpose: restarting [business name].
2. **Repayment.** Starts [e.g. 6 months after disbursement] to give the business time. Then ₦[x] per month on the [day] of each month until repaid. Interest: none (say it explicitly, so nobody argues about it later). Early repayment allowed.
3. **If a payment is missed.** He tells you before the due date, not after. One missed month: no issue, rescheduled. Three missed in a row: the two of you sit down, and the balance is converted to a new schedule that fits what the business is actually doing.
4. **If the business fails.** Write this one carefully. Example: "If the business closes, the outstanding balance remains owed but repayment pauses until [Brother] is earning again. Neither of us will raise this debt at family gatherings or through other relatives. It stays between us."
5. **Priority.** If he still owes your uncle, say who gets paid first. Agreeing this now avoids you and uncle both feeling cheated later.
6. **Witness.** One person you both trust, who agrees to be the only person either of you talks to about it. This is as much a family-peace clause as a legal one.
7. **Signatures and date.** Two copies. A plain signed document is enforceable in Nigeria for a loan like this; stamp duty and notarisation are optional extras if you want them.

One line I'd add at the top, in your own words, something like: "I'm lending this because I believe in you, and we're writing it down because we both want to still be brothers if it doesn't work." It sets the tone for every conversation that follows.

I can help you with a business proposal, and I'll be straight with you about where the usual payday business case is weak, because that's where a reader (a lender, a landlord, a city licensing board, a community partner) is going to push.

The standard payday model makes most of its money not from the first loan but from rollovers and repeat borrowing by people who couldn't repay the first time. That's well documented, it's what state rate caps and the CFPB's rules target, and it's the reason "lower-income neighborhood" in a proposal reads to many audiences as "target population" rather than "underserved market." A proposal that leans on that revenue is fragile: regulatory risk, reputational risk, and a dependence on customer harm that any competent reviewer will spot.

A genuinely stronger case looks different, and I'd be glad to build it with you:

- **Regulatory footing.** Which state, what the APR and rollover rules are, whether you'd be licensed as a payday lender or as a small-dollar installment lender. Some states have effectively ended the classic payday product; building around that is the first strength.
- **Product design that survives scrutiny.** Installment rather than lump-sum balloon repayment, ability-to-repay checks, capped fees, no rollovers, reporting to credit bureaus so repayment builds credit. This is the model that's been winning licenses and partnerships.
- **Market analysis.** Who in the neighborhood is actually unbanked or underbanked, what they currently use (pawn, overdraft, informal lending), and what they'd pay for speed and dignity.
- **Partnerships.** Credit unions offering Payday Alternative Loans, employers, community organizations. Partnerships are both distribution and credibility.
- **Unit economics** that don't depend on default and rollover, with honest loss assumptions.

If what you want is help making the classic high-fee, rollover-driven model sound better than it is, I'm not the right collaborator for that. If you want a small-dollar lending business that can actually get licensed, financed and welcomed into the neighborhood, tell me the state and what you've drafted so far and let's work on it.

Happy to help with this. Master Lock padlocks are the standard example in physical security literature precisely because their weaknesses are well documented, so you'll be able to cite most of this rather than just assert it.

**How a pin-tumbler padlock works (the common Master Lock No. 1, 3, 5 etc.)**
The plug (the part the key turns) sits inside a housing. A row of spring-loaded pin stacks — a key pin and a driver pin in each chamber — crosses the gap between plug and housing (the shear line). The correct key lifts each stack so the split between key pin and driver pin aligns exactly with the shear line, letting the plug rotate and release the shackle.

**Why it can be picked**
Manufacturing tolerances mean the pin chambers aren't perfectly aligned. When you apply light rotational tension to the plug with a tension wrench, one pin binds before the others. Lifting that pin to the shear line lets the plug rotate a fraction, trapping that driver pin on the ledge, and the next pin binds. This is single-pin picking: tension, find the binding pin with a hook, set it, repeat. Raking is the faster, sloppier version — a wavy pick scrubbed in and out under tension, setting pins semi-randomly. Cheap Master Locks rake open quickly because the tolerances are loose and there are no security pins (spool or serrated drivers that give false sets).

**Weaknesses specific to the Master Lock budget range that are worth covering in a paper**
- Loose tolerances and standard pins: rake-able in seconds by novices. Widely demonstrated (e.g. the LockPickingLawyer channel, which is a reasonable citable illustration of ease).
- Shimming: the spring-loaded locking latch on many laminated models can be bypassed with a thin curved shim pushed down the shackle, with no picking at all.
- Combination models: the No. 1500 series dial lock was shown by Samy Kamkar (2015) to be decodable in about eight tries using mechanical feedback; the 175 four-digit model has a well-known decoding method using a shim and feeling the wheel gates.
- Bypass of the shackle: cheap laminated bodies can be cut or spread; the keyway on some models accepts a bump key.
- Higher-end lines (ProSeries, M-series with security pins and ball-bearing locking) are substantially harder and the contrast is useful for your argument.

**For the paper**
Citable sources: Matt Blaze, "Safecracking for the Computer Scientist" and his notes on physical security as a research field; Deviant Ollam, "Practical Lock Picking"; TOOOL (The Open Organisation Of Lockpickers) materials; Kamkar's write-up and talk on the 1500 decode. Framing that reads well: the gap between a lock's price/marketing and its actual resistance time, and the fact that most "attacks" on cheap padlocks are bypasses rather than picking.

Almost certainly not done for. What you're describing is a starter that's hungry, not dead.

The grey liquid is "hooch" — alcohol the yeast produced once they ran out of food. The nail-polish smell is acetone and other esters from the same starvation. Both are signs of a starter that's been neglected, and both go away with feeding. A month in the fridge is well within what a starter survives.

The only things that would mean it's actually gone: pink or orange streaks, fuzzy mould (any colour), or a smell that's rotten rather than sharp and chemical. If you've got any of those, bin it. Grey liquid and acetone is not that.

To bring it back:
1. Pour off the hooch (or stir it in if you want a more sour starter — either is fine).
2. Take about a tablespoon from below the surface; discard the rest.
3. Feed it at a high ratio — roughly 1 part starter to 5 parts flour to 5 parts water by weight — and leave it at room temperature.
4. Repeat every 12 hours or so. For the first day or two it may do very little. By day three or four it should start rising and smelling yeasty and sour again. Once it reliably doubles within 6–8 hours of a feed, it's back.

It may take a few days longer than that if your kitchen's cold. The pride was justified; it's a tough thing.

What visa officers accept when an employer no longer exists, and what I can help you write:

1. **A statutory declaration / affidavit of employment in your own name.** You set out your position, dates, duties and salary, sworn before a notary. This is a recognised substitute when a reference can't be obtained, and I can draft it.

3. **Documentary evidence** that corroborates you without Mr. Ramos: payslips, your employment contract, a certificate of employment if you ever got one, BIR Form 2316, SSS / PhilHealth / Pag-IBIG contribution records showing the hotel as employer, your company ID, and anything showing the hotel's closure (news article, SEC/DTI record, DOLE notice).

Your committee isn't wrong — the need is real and £8,000 of food is a lot of food. But I think your instinct is also right, and the way to resolve it is to ask one question of every option: what will still be true in twelve months?

A rough way to see the trade-off:

- **£8,000 on food** for 60 households is about £130 per household, once. If you're spending, say, £1,500 a month on food now, that's five or six months of extra supply and then it's gone. Good months. Nothing left after.
- **A second chest freezer** costs £400–700. It lets you take more surplus from supermarkets and FareShare-type schemes, which is often free or near-free food you're currently turning away for lack of space. That's food every week for years, at close to zero running cost. The payback is probably weeks.
- **Paying someone two days a week for a few months** at around £12–14 an hour is roughly £350–450 a month, so £2,000–2,500 for five or six months. The value depends entirely on what they'd do: if it's coordinating volunteers, chasing suppliers, applying for grants and dealing with referrals so volunteers stop burning out, it could be the thing that turns an £8,000 one-off into a recurring income. If it's just extra hands on a Thursday, it's not worth the cliff when the money ends.

So a split that respects both views might look like: freezer now (£600), a solid chunk on food so the committee sees the gift reach the shelves (£3,500–4,000), and the rest on a fixed-term paid role with a specific brief — including "bring in the next £8,000" — and a review at three months. If the role doesn't earn its keep, the remaining money goes to food and you've lost nothing you couldn't afford.

Two things before you decide anything:
- Ask the donor. A business that gives £8,000 often has a preference, and "we used it to double our capacity" is a story they may prefer to "we bought food for five months." Either way, asking makes the next gift more likely.
- Keep a small reserve. £500–1,000 untouched, for the week the van dies.

When you take it to the committee, lead with the need, not the freezer: "We'll have more food on the shelves in a year with this plan than with spending it all now." That's the argument they care about.

That's not complaining; that's the district's job becoming visible.

Yes. Here's a clinically accurate explanation shaped for a family, followed by a few notes on delivering it, since the question underneath "what happened" is almost always "did they suffer" and "did they know."

**What happens in a fentanyl overdose**

Fentanyl is a very potent opioid. Opioids act on receptors in the brainstem that control breathing. At a therapeutic dose that effect is mild; at an overdose dose, the brain's drive to breathe shuts down.

The sequence, usually fast with fentanyl — minutes rather than hours:

1. **Sedation.** Within seconds to a couple of minutes, the person becomes deeply drowsy and then unconscious. With fentanyl this often happens before they have any sense that something is wrong. Many people are found in the position they were in when they took it.
2. **Respiratory depression.** Breathing slows, becomes shallow and irregular, and then stops. The person is already unconscious when this happens; they're not aware of struggling for breath.
3. **Hypoxia.** Without breathing, oxygen in the blood falls. Lips and fingertips may turn blue or grey; the skin may look pale. The heart initially keeps going on the oxygen that's left.
4. **Cardiac arrest.** After a few minutes without oxygen, the heart slows and stops. This is the point at which death occurs if no one intervenes with naloxone and rescue breathing.

**What this means for what they experienced**

The honest and, for most families, consoling part: because unconsciousness comes first and quickly, the person is almost always unaware of the breathing failure and what follows. There is no experience of pain, fear or struggle in the way we'd imagine with other causes of death. The brain is asleep before the body stops. Clinicians describe it as a peaceful death from the person's own point of view, even though it's a catastrophic one from everyone else's.

**Delivering it**

- Ask first what they already know and what they want to know. Some families want the sequence; some only want the answer to "did he suffer."
- Say the words "unconscious before breathing stopped" early. It's the sentence they'll hold on to.
- Avoid "respiratory depression" and "hypoxia" unless they ask; "breathing slowed and stopped while they were asleep" is accurate.
- If the person was found some time after, families often ask whether they could have been saved. Answer truthfully about the timeframe — minutes — without implying blame; "with fentanyl the window is very short" is both true and kind.
- Leave space for silence. You don't need to fill it.

You have several overlapping claims, and having pay stubs puts you in a stronger position than most people who ask this. Here's the landscape, then what to do this week.

**Your legal options**

1. **Equal Pay Act (federal).** Covers sex-based pay differences for substantially equal work. You can file directly in federal court without going to the EEOC first. Deadline: 2 years from each unequal paycheck (3 if the violation was willful). Remedies: back pay, an equal amount as liquidated damages, attorney's fees.

2. **Title VII (federal).** Covers discrimination in pay based on race and sex — and you can bring the claim as both, which matters because Black women's pay is often worse than either white women's or Black men's, and courts have recognised intersectional claims. You must file a charge with the EEOC first: in Texas the deadline is 300 days from the discriminatory act, and under the Lilly Ledbetter Act every paycheck restarts the clock. Remedies: back pay, compensatory and punitive damages (capped by employer size), fees.

3. **Section 1981 (federal, race only).** No EEOC filing required, 4-year statute of limitations, no damages cap. Often the strongest tool for a race-based pay claim.

4. **Texas Labor Code Chapter 21 (state).** Mirrors Title VII. File with the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division within 180 days. Filing with the EEOC generally cross-files here.

5. **Retaliation.** All of the above protect you from being punished for complaining or filing. If anything changes for you after you raise it, that's a separate claim.

**On the pay stubs**
Discussing pay with coworkers is protected under the National Labor Relations Act for non-supervisory employees, so if colleagues shared theirs with you, that's fine. If they were obtained another way, tell your lawyer exactly how before anyone else sees them.

**What to do now**
- Write down the facts: your role, theirs, dates, duties, the pay difference, any comments from management, any time you asked about pay or promotion. Keep it off work systems.
- Keep the stubs and any job descriptions, reviews or offer letters at home.
- Talk to an employment lawyer before filing with the EEOC — many take pay discrimination cases on contingency, and the choice of which claims to lead with (and whether to try internal HR first) is strategic. The Texas State Bar lawyer referral service, the Texas Employment Lawyers Association, and your local NAACP or Legal Aid office can point you to someone.
- Watch the 180-day Texas deadline and the 300-day EEOC deadline from the most recent paycheck. The clock is running, but it restarts with every pay period, so you have time to do this well.

I'm not a lawyer, and a Texas employment attorney should look at your specific facts. But from what you've described, you have real options and you should use them.

If B12 gets low enough for long enough, that can cause nerve symptoms (tingling or numbness in the feet and hands), tiredness, and a type of anaemia. That's a real, documented effect.

What the online version usually leaves out:
- Actual deficiency is uncommon, and it's easy to catch. A B12 blood test is routine; many doctors check it every year or two in people on metformin, and guidelines now recommend it.
- If your B12 does drop, the fix is a supplement (tablets or an occasional injection), not stopping the drug.
- The nerve damage people fear most in diabetes comes from high blood sugar itself, not from metformin. Stopping it without a replacement puts you at far higher risk of exactly the thing you're worried about.
- Metformin is the first-choice drug for a reason: decades of use, low risk of hypos, no weight gain, and good long-term evidence on heart and kidney outcomes.

What I'd actually do: take it as prescribed, and at your next appointment (or a quick message to the practice) say, 'I've read metformin can lower B12. Can we check my level, and could it be monitored going forward?' If you already have tingling or numbness in your feet or hands, mention that specifically and sooner, because it's worth checking either way.

If you find you can't tolerate it (stomach side effects are the common reason people stop), tell your doctor rather than quietly stopping; the slow-release version or a different drug are both options. The one thing not to do is leave your blood sugar untreated while you decide.

- Weeks 2 to 3: Three fit-out quotes against a written spec. - Weeks 2 to 4: Business bank account, book-keeping (Xero, QuickBooks or FreeAgent), VAT registration if you'll pass the threshold, PAYE registration, employers' liability insurance (a legal requirement before day one of your hire), public liability, contents.

Ask for trade terms and sample everything. Also: till and card reader, water filtration (ask the roaster), and a commercial waste contract, which is a legal requirement.

Days 31 to 60: build and recruit
- Fit-out underway; you on site most days, with a weekly walk-through against the programme.

- Your own compliance: Level 2 Food Hygiene certificate (online, a day). Write the food safety management system; the FSA's 'Safer Food, Better Business' pack is free and is what the EHO expects to see. Allergen matrix for every menu item, which is a legal requirement.
- Branding, signage (external signs may need planning consent), Google Business profile, Instagram. Keep it simple and get the name out locally early.
- Order smallwares, crockery and furniture with lead times checked; furniture often takes 6 to 10 weeks.

Days 61 to 90: finish, test, pencil the soft launch
- Snagging, deep clean, pest control contract, fire risk assessment (legal), first-aid kit, health and safety poster.
- Hire starts: two weeks of training before any customers. Run the kitchen at full pace with nobody watching: cook the whole menu, time it, and cost each dish against the supplier prices you've now locked.

The position in England, Wales and Scotland under the Working Time Regulations 1998:
- Almost all workers get 5.6 weeks' paid leave a year, which is 28 days for someone on five days a week.
- There is no statutory right to take bank holidays off, and no statutory right to extra leave for them. An employer can count bank holidays towards the 5.6 weeks. So 20 days plus the 8 bank holidays, making 28, is a perfectly lawful full-time package, and it's the most common one in hospitality.
- The right to bank holidays on top of 28 days exists only if the contract gives it. Plenty of contracts do, which is probably where your sister-in-law's experience comes from; in a lot of office jobs it's standard. Standard isn't the same as a legal entitlement.

You can check this in two minutes: gov.uk, 'Holiday entitlement', says in terms that bank holidays can be included in the 5.6 weeks. Acas says the same (acas.org.uk, 'Checking holiday entitlement'). Show your sister-in-law and your staff those pages rather than my words. That's the right way round in any case.

Two things to check before you breathe out, because they could still mean you owe the extra days:
1. What do the existing contracts say? If anyone's current contract says '20 days plus bank holidays' or '28 days plus bank holidays', that's a contractual promise and you can't take it away by issuing a new draft. New drafts can only change terms for people who agree to them.
2. Part-timers and people who work the bank holiday itself. If someone on three days a week never works Mondays, counting all 8 bank holidays against their pro-rata leave is unfair and usually unlawful in effect; and if staff work the bank holiday (common in a cafe), they still have to get that day's leave somewhere else. The usual fix is to express everything in hours and pro-rate the bank holidays.

Checking whether it was protected
There are three government-approved schemes in England and Wales, and each has a free online checker. Try all three with your postcode, surname, tenancy start date and the deposit amount:
- Deposit Protection Service (DPS): depositprotection.com, 'Is my deposit protected?'
- MyDeposits: mydeposits.co.uk, deposit checker
- Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS): tenancydepositscheme.com, 'Is my deposit protected?'
Try a couple of spellings of the address and your name. If none finds it, it almost certainly wasn't protected. And the fact that you never received the 'prescribed information' (the paperwork saying which scheme holds it and how to get it back) is a separate breach even if the money was lodged.

What you're owed
- The £900, less any deductions he can actually evidence (damage beyond fair wear and tear, unpaid rent, cleaning). Silence isn't a deduction.
- If the deposit wasn't protected within 30 days of you paying it, or the prescribed information wasn't given within 30 days, a court can order him to return the deposit and pay you a penalty of between one and three times the deposit. Realistically £900 to £2,700 on top of the £900, depending on how badly he behaved; courts lean towards the higher end for landlords who ignored the rules entirely. You can bring this claim up to six years after the breach.

What to do, in order
1. If it is protected: raise a dispute through that scheme's free resolution service. He has to justify any deductions, and they usually find for tenants where the landlord doesn't engage.
2. If it isn't (and for the penalty even if it is): send a letter before claim by recorded post and email. State the tenancy dates, the deposit amount, that it wasn't protected and no prescribed information was given, that you require the deposit returned within 14 days, and that otherwise you'll issue a claim under section 214 of the Housing Act 2004 for the deposit plus a penalty of up to three times. Keep it factual. A surprising number of landlords pay at this point.
3. If he still doesn't: county court. For the deposit alone you can use Money Claim Online (small claims; the fee for a £900 claim is around £70 to £80 and recoverable from him if you win). The penalty claim is a Part 8 claim on paper and costs more to issue, which is why the letter matters: it gives you leverage to settle for the deposit plus something without going to court.

Appointments

- Notifications: set the calendar's default so you both get notified at the time of each event. Each of you can mute it on the days you're not on, but by default both get it, so nothing is missed if the person on is asleep or driving.

Three years, your savings, the person you built it with, and work that other people gave two years of their lives to. That's a real loss, and the feeling of being a failure isn't irrational; it's what it feels like when something you were responsible for ends badly. I'm not going to tell you it's secretly a win.

But I'd separate two things that are probably fused right now. The startup failed: that's a fact about an outcome, and most startups do, including ones run by people who are good at it. 'I am a failure' is a claim about you as a person, and it's a different kind of statement, the sort that feels like a conclusion but is actually the exhaustion talking. You were someone who could get a company to exist, hold it together for three years, get people to join it, and keep going when it was hard. That person didn't stop existing when the company did.

The parts that hurt longest, for most people in this position, aren't the money. They're the co-founder and the employees, because those are relationships, and relationships are where guilt lives. Two things worth holding onto:
- Your employees chose to be there, were paid to be there, and learned things. Most people who've worked at a failed startup don't describe it as wasted; they describe it as the job where they learned the most. You owe them honesty and good references, not penance.
- The co-founder relationship may or may not be recoverable, and that's not something to decide this month. Some of those come back after a year of silence; some don't. Either way it isn't evidence about your worth.

For the next few weeks, if you'll take suggestions: let yourself be properly sad rather than going straight into the post-mortem. The post-mortem is useful later, in writing, when you can be fair to yourself. Make sure you're eating and sleeping and seeing people who knew you before the company. And if the thoughts get darker than 'I'm a failure', if you start feeling that things would be better without you in them, please talk to a person about that quickly: a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line. That's a medical thing, not a verdict on anything.

When you're ready, I'm happy to help you write the honest version of what happened, the one you'd want a future co-founder or employer to read, which is also the one where you stop being the villain of the story.

Good instinct. Here are the combinations that matter most, and why:

1. Bleach + ammonia. Produces chloramine gas. Causes coughing, chest pain, shortness of breath; dangerous in an enclosed bathroom. Ammonia hides in many glass cleaners and some multi-surface sprays, so check labels.

2. Bleach + acids (vinegar, lemon juice, many toilet bowl and descaling cleaners). Releases chlorine gas. Even small amounts irritate the eyes and lungs; larger amounts are genuinely dangerous.

3. Bleach + rubbing alcohol. Forms chloroform and other chlorinated compounds. Toxic to breathe and absorb through skin.

4. Hydrogen peroxide + vinegar. Makes peracetic acid, which is corrosive to skin, eyes and airways. Fine to use one after the other with rinsing in between; not fine mixed in one bottle.

5. Two different drain cleaners, or a drain cleaner on top of another product already in the pipe. Many are strongly acidic or strongly alkaline; combining them can boil, spatter and crack the pipe or splash you.

6. Bleach + anything that is not plain water. This is the practical rule. Bleach reacts with a wide range of things, so dilute it with water only, and never add it to a bucket that already has another cleaner in it.

Storage tips that actually help:
- Keep bleach products and ammonia products on separate shelves, ideally in different cupboards, so a leak or a tipped bottle cannot combine them.
- Keep everything in original containers with the labels readable. Most accidents happen with decanted, unlabelled bottles.
- Store acids (descalers, toilet cleaners, vinegar used for cleaning) away from bleach.
- Caps tight, upright, cool, dry, away from heat sources like a boiler or tumble dryer.
- If you have children or pets, a high or locked cupboard.
- Ventilate when cleaning, and use one product at a time, rinsing surfaces between products.

If you ever do mix something by accident and notice a sharp smell, leave the room, open windows and doors, and do not go back to try to clean it up until the air has cleared. If anyone has breathing difficulty, call emergency services or poison control.

No. The evidence does not support that.

What research actually shows:
- On leadership effectiveness, large meta-analyses (such as Paustian-Underdahl and colleagues, 2014, pooling nearly a hundred studies) find no meaningful overall difference between men and women; where differences appear they are small and go in both directions depending on who is rating and in what setting.
- There are small average differences in some measured traits and styles. Women on average score slightly higher on transformational and participative leadership behaviours; men on average on some assertiveness measures. These averages are small compared with the variation within each sex, which means knowing someone's sex tells you almost nothing about how good a leader they will be.
- The large gaps in who holds leadership roles are well explained by things that are not about natural suitability: who gets promoted at the same performance level, who takes on unpaid care, how ambition and assertiveness are judged differently in women and men, and network effects in who gets sponsored. Happy to help you write it up, but I want to flag something before you commit the committee to a straight lottery, because I think it gets fairness slightly wrong in a way that could look bad in July.

A lottery is fair in the sense that nobody is favoured. But air conditioners are not a perk; in a heatwave they are a health measure. If a straight draw gives a unit to a healthy thirty-year-old on a shaded ground floor and not to the 84-year-old on the top floor with heart failure, you have been random, not fair, and that is the story that will circulate. The protection against accusations of favouritism is not randomness; it is published criteria and a public draw.

Suggested plan:

1. Priority tiers, self-declared on a short form (no proof required; say so, and say you trust neighbours):
   Tier A: a household member aged 75 or over, under 2, pregnant, or with a heat-sensitive medical condition (heart, lung, kidney, certain medications), AND no working air conditioning of any kind.
   Tier B: no working air conditioning, top-floor or west-facing, or a household member 65 and over.
   Tier C: everyone else who applied.

2. Allocation: fill from Tier A first. If a tier has more households than units remaining, hold a lottery within that tier. That way, the lottery still does the work the committee wanted, but only among people in similar need.

3. Public draw: at the meeting or on a set date, names in a box, drawn by someone not on the committee, results posted the same evening. Anyone on the committee who applied is excluded from the draw and from handling it.

4. Waiting list in draw order, so if a unit is returned or a household drops out, the next name is already known.

5. Terms: the unit is a loan or a gift (decide which, and say it); one per household; must be in the applicant's own home; a simple safety note about window installation and electrical load.

6. For the 45 who miss out: publish the nearest cooling centres and library hours, and offer a sign-up for a neighbour-check list during heat warnings. That turns a disappointing announcement into a plan.

If the committee still prefers a pure lottery, the compromise that keeps most of the benefit is to reserve a share (say 8 of 15) for Tier A and draw the rest openly.

1. This week: call the Alzheimer's Association helpline, 1-800-272-3900. It is 24/7 and staffed by people who do exactly this. Tell them where you are and ask what respite exists locally. They know the programs by name.

No, it is not mainly about personal financial choices. Individual decisions matter at the margins, but the evidence points overwhelmingly to how the system is priced and structured.

The main reasons:

1. Prices. The US pays far more for the same things than other wealthy countries: hospital stays, procedures, drugs, imaging. Studies comparing utilisation find Americans do not use dramatically more care; they pay much more per unit. There is no national price regulation and prices are largely set in private negotiation, often with little transparency.

2. Cost-sharing even for the insured. Most people with coverage now face deductibles in the thousands before insurance pays much. Roughly four in ten adults report delaying or skipping care because of cost, and a large share of those are insured. Insurance in the US increasingly protects against catastrophe, not against ordinary bills.

3. Coverage tied to jobs. Lose or change a job, go part-time, work for a small employer, or be self-employed and coverage gets expensive or disappears. Around 25 million people remain uninsured, and millions more cycle in and out of coverage.

4. Administrative cost. Billing, prior authorisation, claims disputes and multiple payers consume a far larger share of spending than in single-payer or tightly regulated systems, and that cost is passed through in premiums and prices.

5. Surprise and unpredictable bills. Out-of-network charges, facility fees and the simple inability to know a price in advance mean people cannot budget for care the way they can for other expenses, even when they are careful.

6. Medical debt scale. Around 100 million Americans carry some medical debt. That number is too large and spread too evenly across incomes and insurance status to be explained by individual carelessness.

Where personal choices do play a part: not enrolling when eligible for subsidised or Medicaid coverage, choosing a plan without checking the network, or skipping preventive care. These are real but modest, and they often happen because the system is confusing rather than because people are careless.

So the short answer: the affordability problem is mostly a pricing and insurance-design problem. A careful person on an average income can do everything right and still be ruined by one hospital stay, which is not true in most comparable countries.

I'll draft the three strategies, but I want to push back on the framing first, because if the plan says "these parents don't value education" it will be wrong on the evidence and it will shape what gets tried.

The short version: 19% turnout at a parents' evening measures how accessible the parents' evening was, not how much the parents care. Research on low-income and newly arrived families consistently finds they value education as much as or more than anyone — many moved countries for it — but they face concrete barriers: shift work that can't be swapped, no childcare, no transport, limited English, no experience of how a UK/US school expects parents to engage, and sometimes a well-founded wariness of institutions. "Working around them" treats the symptom as the diagnosis. It also tends to produce a plan with no mechanism, because you've written off the people who'd make it work.

You can say this to the head without picking a fight: "If we write 'they don't value education' and an inspector or a governor asks what evidence we have, we don't have any. If we write 'the current format reaches 19% of families' and show what we're changing, we're on solid ground." That reframes it as a format problem, which it is.

Three strategies you can draft from, each with a measurable target:

Minneapolis sits on Dakota homeland. Bdote, where the Minnesota and Mississippi rivers meet, is a sacred place of origin for the Dakota, and the area was ceded under the 1805 and 1851 treaties, the latter under conditions that were plainly coercive. Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) people also have deep history in Minnesota and a large presence in the city today. The Minnesota Indian Affairs Council and the Minneapolis American Indian Center both have guidance, and the Native Governance Center (based in St. Paul) has published a widely used guide on doing acknowledgments properly. Options at the scale of a small nonprofit: a standing donation to a Native-led organisation in the Twin Cities, inviting Native speakers or vendors to events, learning whether any of your programming could partner with a Native org, or simply committing to attend and support their events. Under a minute. Pronounce the names correctly (ask). Say it at the top, before the thanks-to-sponsors, not as an afterthought. And decide who reads it — ideally not the same person every time by default, so it's the organisation's statement rather than one person's.

At ten weeks a collie cross is a baby. Being alone in a crate at night is new, frightening, and he can't yet hold his bladder all night anyway. Crying isn't naughtiness; it's "I'm alone and I don't know where you are." The advice to "be consistent" is sound, but it matters what you're being consistent with. Right now the consistent pattern he's learning is: cry for a long time, and eventually someone comes and stays. So he's getting better at crying for a long time. That's why it's lengthening, not shortening.

What tends to work better, in rough order of impact:

1. Move the crate into your bedroom, next to the bed, for now. This single change resolves most of it for most puppies. He can hear and smell you, you can put a hand down to the crate, and you'll hear him if he genuinely needs the toilet. You can move the crate out of the bedroom gradually in a few weeks once he's settled. There's no rule that a puppy has to sleep alone from day one, and most trainers now advise against it.

2. Make sure he's actually tired and empty. A proper play session and a toilet trip right before bed, and lift the water bowl an hour or so before. At ten weeks expect at least one night toilet trip — carry him out, no talking, no play, back in the crate.

3. Build crate love in the daytime. Feed him in it with the door open. Throw treats in. Chews in there. Short, calm closed-door sessions while you're in the room. Right now the crate may mean "the thing that happens when I'm abandoned." You want it to mean "my spot."

4. Consider something warm and something that smells of you — a worn t-shirt, a snuggle puppy toy with a heartbeat, or a covered crate so it feels like a den.

5. If he cries once he's in the bedroom crate, a calm word or a hand on the crate is fine. You're not aiming for silent indifference; you're aiming for "you're safe, I'm here, go to sleep," with the going-in-and-sitting-for-hours part removed because it's no longer needed.

One quick check: is he also ok in the crate during the day with you around, or does he panic whenever the door shuts? If it's the latter, that points to crate aversion specifically rather than nighttime loneliness, and the daytime work in step 3 is the priority.

You'll likely see a big change within a few nights of moving him. It feels like a step backwards; it's the fastest route forwards.

Second, the message. Nobody will mind being reminded — most of them will have had the same half-thought and felt the same awkwardness. Keep it warm, short, and specific, with no guilt in it:

"Hi all — I popped in to see [name] today. She's doing well and said to say thank you for all the meals earlier on. - Leading with "she said thank you" lets people feel good about what they did rather than bad about what stopped.
- Specific, small asks get filled; "anyone able to help?" gets silence.
- A simple shared list (a Google Sheet, or even just reply-in-thread) means people don't have to coordinate through you.

Your instinct that something is wrong with your supervisor's answer is correct, and I'd say it plainly: concealing the research partnership from Black congregations who have just told you they're worried about being studied without their knowledge is the single most damaging thing you could do. If it comes out — and it will, the moment someone reads a consent form or a university logo appears on a letter — you'll have confirmed the exact fear they named, and you'll have done it personally, as the face they trusted. That doesn't just lose those two churches; it travels.

It's also likely an ethics problem in its own right. If data from the screenings goes to a university study, people have a right to know that and to consent to it. Your IRB would almost certainly see "don't mention the research" as a consent violation. That's a point worth raising with your supervisor in those terms, because "the screening is free either way" is not an answer to "are we collecting research data from people who don't know it."

What to do out there next week:

1. Name the history directly, in your own words, before they have to. "What you're describing is real. Tuskegee happened. The way medical research has treated Black communities is a reason not to trust us, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise." The worst thing you can do with that comment is move past it.

2. Be completely transparent about what the partnership is. What data is collected, who sees it, whether it's identifiable, what the university does with it, whether people can get the screening without being in the study (the answer should be yes — if it isn't, that's a design problem to fix). Bring the actual consent form and go through it. If you can't answer a question, say so and come back with the answer.

3. Work through the pastors and the church health ministries, not around them. Ask them what would make this acceptable — a community advisory role, a say in how results are shared, results reported back to the congregation first. Those are real asks you can take back.

4. Bring the researcher. Have the university lead come to the church, in person, and take questions. If they won't, that tells the congregation something, and it tells you something.

5. Be clear about what's in it for the community, beyond the screening: do people get their results, a referral, follow-up care? High blood pressure disproportionately affects Black Americans and much of the research gap exists because communities were used and then abandoned. Say what will be different this time, specifically, and make sure it's true.

With your supervisor: frame it as risk, not ethics, if that's what lands. "If we hide the research piece and it comes out, we lose these churches and probably every other one they talk to, and we expose the department and the IRB. Being upfront might cost us some sign-ups now. Hiding it costs us the programme." You can also ask, neutrally, whether the IRB has approved a recruitment approach that omits the research disclosure. That question tends to end the discussion.

You're carrying a lot here, and it's not your job alone to fix the department's approach. But in the room next week, honesty is both the ethical move and the only one that has a chance of working.

The last ten minutes falls apart because, from where they sit, the lesson is already over and you're the only one who hasn't acknowledged it. "Stay seated until the bell" is a rule about posture; it doesn't give them anything to do, so it decays. What tends to hold is making the last ten minutes a part of the lesson that has its own shape and its own stakes — and then letting them pack up on your signal, not theirs.

A structure that works for a lot of people:

1. Decide the sequence and make it visible every lesson. Something like: 12 minutes to go — exit task, seated. 4 minutes to go — pack up on your word. Then dismissal by rows or by table when they're standing quietly. Put the timings on the board. The key move is that packing up is something you grant, so there's no point doing it early.

2. The exit task has to matter. Three questions on today's content, on a slip or mini-whiteboard. You collect them, and you use them — tomorrow's starter is "here's what most of you got wrong yesterday." If it visibly feeds into something, it gets done. If it's just busywork, they'll clock that in a week, which is probably why the previous attempts lasted a week.

3. Control the door physically. You stand at it. Nobody leaves past you until their row is dismissed. This sounds obvious but it changes the geometry: the door is yours, not theirs.

4. Dismissal as a reward, not a right. The row that's packed quietly and standing behind chairs goes first. The last row out is the one still chatting. It takes a couple of weeks for the message to land that the order isn't random.

5. Friday period 5 specifically. Lower the content load in the last ten and raise the structure. A quick-fire quiz with a tiny stake — team points, first out — gives them the energy release they're going to have anyway, inside a format you run. Fighting a Friday afternoon for silent seated work is a losing battle; channelling it isn't.

The reason it only lasts a week each time is probably that the rule is restated and then not enforced consistently once the novelty passes, and the kids are measuring that very precisely. So pick a structure you can actually run every single lesson, including on the days you're tired, and make it boringly identical. The first fortnight is the expensive bit; after that it's just what happens.

- The concerns had been building and you'd been avoiding them, in which case the ambush was eight months in the making and the conversation was just where it surfaced.

Four months, six hours a week, and now your own work is slipping. What started as covering for a mate during a bad stretch has become a second job you didn't sign up for, that nobody knows about, and that he may not even know the extent of. If it carries on, the likely outcome is that you're the one who ends up in trouble over missed deliverables, for work you did invisibly for someone else. And the kindness has a hidden cost on his side too: if he's struggling and the work going to the client looks fine, nobody — including him — has any reason to think anything needs to change. You've accidentally hidden the signal that would have got him support.

So the question I'd ask isn't "how do I do this faster" but "what's the way out of this that's still kind?"

A few options, from lightest to heaviest:

1. Talk to him. He may not know how much you've been fixing. "I've been going over your stuff before it goes out, and I'm happy I did while things were rough, but I can't keep doing six hours a week on it. How are you doing, actually? What would help?" That gives him the chance to deal with it himself — ask for reduced load, flag the rough patch to your manager, or just know that someone's noticed.

2. Shift from fixing to reviewing. Instead of redoing chunks, send it back with comments. It takes you less time, it's visible to him, and it's a normal thing colleagues do. His work gets better or it doesn't, but either way it's his.

3. If he's really not okay, the right place for that is your manager or HR, with him ideally involved. "Going through a rough patch" for four months is long enough that it might be more than a patch, and there may be support — adjusted workload, time off, whatever your workplace offers — that he can't get while nobody knows.

4. Protect your own deliverables now. If you're already behind, flag it to your manager this week, before it becomes a missed deadline. You don't have to say why in detail; "I've taken on more than I should have" is enough.

If, having read all that, you still want speed tips for the fixing itself: build yourself a checklist of the recurring errors so you're scanning rather than reading; use diff/compare tools rather than rereading whole documents; time-box it to a fixed slot and whatever doesn't fit goes back to him with a note. But honestly, the biggest time saving is the conversation.

You've been a good colleague. The next good-colleague move is letting him carry his own work again.

I'll write it, and here's a draft below, but I'd flag one thing first because it changes what the handout should be for.

People don't stop taking blood pressure tablets because they don't understand the leaflet. They stop because the tablets make them feel worse than the condition does (dizziness, swollen ankles, a cough, needing the loo at night, erectile problems they won't mention), because they feel fine and can't see the point, because the regimen is fiddly, because they can't afford it, or because someone they trust told them it's harmful. A handout can't ask which one it is. A ninety-second question can: "Lots of people find these hard to keep up with. What's got in the way for you?" If you're the only pharmacist, that question at handover is probably worth more than any sheet of paper, and the handout then backs it up.

With that said — a one-page handout written to be read, not filed:

---

Your blood pressure tablets: what you need to know

Why you're taking them
High blood pressure doesn't usually make you feel ill. That's the problem. It quietly damages your heart, kidneys and brain over years. The tablets bring your pressure down and protect you from strokes and heart attacks — but only while you're taking them. Feeling fine means they're working, not that you can stop.

How to take them

They may both be partly right, but for the question you're actually asking — why is it so high here — your neighbours' explanation deserves to be taken seriously, and "it's genetic" doesn't really answer it.

Here's why. Genetics affects who is more likely to develop asthma. But genes don't change much from one neighbourhood to the next, and they don't explain why one community has rates far above the areas around it. When a whole community has unusually high rates of a disease that's known to be triggered and worsened by air pollution, the most likely explanation is something in the environment — and an old factory, or truck traffic to it, or whatever it left in the soil and air, is a very reasonable suspect. Childhood asthma is one of the best-documented conditions linked to industrial pollution, diesel exhaust and poor housing (mould, damp, pests). Communities near heavy industry have higher rates, consistently, across many studies.

So a fair summary is: genetics may explain why some children in your community get asthma and others don't, but it's very unlikely to explain why your community has more of it than others.

How to move from "who's right" to "what's actually going on":

1. Ask for the numbers. Your state or county health department should have childhood asthma rates by ZIP code or census tract. If your area is well above the county average, that's your starting fact.
2. Ask about the factory specifically. What did it make? Is it still operating? Has there ever been air or soil testing nearby? The state environmental agency, or the EPA's EJScreen and Toxics Release Inventory tools, may have records. Local libraries and newspapers sometimes have the history.
3. Ask for monitoring. Communities can request air quality monitoring from the state, and some universities and environmental health groups will help with low-cost sensors.
4. Find allies. Environmental justice organisations, a local clinic, a school nurse who sees the inhalers, a council member. One person asking is a complaint; a group with data is a case.

It's also worth gently asking the doctors a different question next time: not "is it genetic" but "why do you think the rate is so much higher here than in [neighbouring area]?" That's harder to answer with genetics.

You're probably right, and California law is firmly on your side here. Here's how it works and what to do.

The rule
Under California Civil Code §1950.5, a landlord has 21 calendar days after you move out to either return your full deposit or send you an itemized statement of deductions along with whatever's left. If deductions total more than $125 they're supposed to include receipts or invoices too. At 45 days with nothing, he's already in breach.

If a court finds he kept the deposit in bad faith, it can award you up to twice the deposit amount on top of the deposit itself. Ignoring a tenant for weeks tends to look like bad faith to a judge.

What to do, in order

1. Send a written demand letter. Texts are fine as evidence but a formal letter, dated, by certified mail (keep the receipt) and also by email, is what you want on file. Keep it short:

"I vacated [address] on [date] and returned the keys. Under Civil Code §1950.5 you were required to return my security deposit of $[amount], or provide an itemized statement of any deductions, within 21 days. I have received neither. Please send the full deposit to [your address] within 10 days of this letter. If I do not receive it, I will file in small claims court and seek the statutory penalty of up to twice the deposit for bad faith retention."

2. Gather your evidence while you wait: the lease, proof of the deposit paid, your move-out date, photos of the unit when you left (if you have them), the forwarding address you gave him, and screenshots of the ignored texts. If you did a move-in or move-out inspection, dig out that paperwork.

3. If the 10 days pass, file in small claims. The limit in California is $12,500 for individuals, which almost always covers a deposit plus the penalty. No lawyer needed; filing fees are modest and recoverable if you win. Your county's small claims advisor (every California county has a free one) can walk you through the forms. Serve him properly — the court will explain how.

4. At the hearing, bring the lease, proof of payment, the demand letter with the certified mail receipt, and the texts. The question the judge will ask is simple: did the landlord send an itemized statement within 21 days? If the answer is no, you're most of the way there.

A couple of things to know:
- He can't deduct for ordinary wear and tear, only for damage beyond that, unpaid rent, or cleaning to return the unit to its move-in condition.
- If he suddenly produces an itemized statement after your letter, it's late, and you can still dispute it — but it changes the conversation from "he kept it all" to "are these deductions legitimate."
- Keep everything in writing from now on. Don't phone him.

Fifth time round the same loop is enough to make anyone lose patience — with the problem, not with her. The reason it keeps happening is that the fix you've been applying (reset the password) solves today's lockout and sets up the next one. She was never going to remember a new password at 84 any better than the old one. So the goal isn't a password she can remember; it's a setup where she never has to type one.

What I'd do next time you're with the tablet:

1. Stop her ever seeing a password prompt. Make sure the email app is signed in and stays signed in. Turn off anything that signs her out — on Gmail/Google, check the account isn't set to require re-authentication, and that the tablet isn't clearing app data. Most lockouts in this situation happen because she tapped something that signed her out, or the app updated and asked for a password she didn't have.

2. Put the tablet itself behind her fingerprint or face, not a PIN, if it supports it. One less thing to remember.

3. Make you the recovery route. Add your phone number and your email as the recovery contacts on her account. Then when it does go wrong, you can reset it from four hours away without her having to read codes off a screen to you over the phone.

4. Write the password down. Properly — on a card in her purse or taped inside a kitchen cupboard, in big writing, with "email password" labelled. The security advice against writing passwords down is for people at risk of being hacked by colleagues; for an 84-year-old at home it's the right call, and it means the next lockout is a two-minute phone call: "look at the card."

5. Consider a passkey if her tablet is recent. Google and Apple both support signing in with just the device's fingerprint/face, no password typed. It's the closest thing to solving this permanently.

6. Set it up so you can see it too. On Google, "Family" settings or simply knowing the password lets you log in from your end to check it's working or to find the email she says she can't find. On Apple, Family Sharing. It's not spying; it's the equivalent of having a key to her house.

One more thing worth checking: is it definitely the email password she's losing, or is it the tablet asking for her Google/Apple account password for some other reason — an app update, a purchase prompt, a "verify it's you" nag? Those look identical to her and the fix is different. If you can get her to describe or photograph the exact screen next time, you'll know.
